title: Applicant Tracking System Glossary for Small Business Employers
summary: An applicant tracking system, or ATS, is software that manages hiring from job posting through offer in a single platform. For a small or growing business comparing platforms for the first time, the harder problem usually isn't finding an ATS…
body_markdown:
An applicant tracking system, or ATS, is software that manages hiring from job posting through offer in a single platform. For a small or growing business comparing platforms for the first time, the harder problem usually isn't finding an ATS to demo. It's understanding the vocabulary well enough to tell one vendor's pitch apart from another's, especially when nobody on staff has done this kind of procurement before.


This glossary defines 22 terms an SMB employer runs into while evaluating an ATS, organized into six groups: core concepts, system types, screening mechanics, compliance and reporting, evaluation criteria, and implementation. It's compiled by Asure, which also builds Asure Recruiting, an applicant tracking system designed for employers who have outgrown spreadsheet-based hiring but don't have a dedicated HR technology team to manage a complicated purchase.


## How These Terms Fit Together


ATS evaluation for a small or midsize business is a vocabulary problem before it's a vendor problem. If you can't tell an ATS from an HRIS, or a native integration from a file-based one, it's hard to sit through a demo and know what you're actually being sold.


The terms below build on each other in a rough sequence. Core concepts explain what an ATS does day to day. System types (ATS, HRIS, HCM, payroll software) clarify which system actually owns which data, since most vendor confusion starts here. Screening and ranking mechanics show how candidates get filtered before a person looks at them, which in turn determines which compliance obligations apply. Evaluation criteria and implementation vocabulary carry that understanding into an actual purchase decision, covering what belongs on a scorecard, what to ask in a demo, and what to confirm before signing. Work through the sections in order and you end up with a vendor choice you can explain to a business partner, not just one that felt right after a good sales call.


## Core Concepts


### Applicant Tracking System (ATS)


An applicant tracking system, or ATS, is software that manages the hiring process from job posting through offer in a single platform, replacing the mix of email threads, spreadsheets, and sticky notes on a monitor most small teams start with. It typically handles distributing job postings, collecting applications, screening candidates, scheduling interviews, and tracking offers, all in one place that every hiring manager involved can see without asking someone else for an update.


For most small businesses, the point where an ATS starts paying for itself is when hiring volume outpaces what a shared inbox and a spreadsheet can reliably track. Asure Recruiting is one example built for that stage of growth: it manages the hiring workflow and connects directly into AsureCentral, so a signed offer becomes a new-hire record in payroll and HR without anyone retyping compensation, start date, or job classification. For a closer look at when switching off spreadsheets makes financial sense, see[Are Applicant Tracking Systems Worth It for Small Businesses?](https://www.asuresoftware.com/are-applicant-tracking-systems-worth-it/)


Related terms: Requisition, Candidate Pipeline, HRIS, Implementation Timeline


### Requisition


A requisition is the record inside an ATS for one open position. It usually includes the job title, department, hiring manager, approved headcount, and current status, and it functions as the anchor that every application, interview note, and offer for that role gets attached to.


A single requisition for a high-volume hourly role, such as a seasonal retail or warehouse position, can draw a large batch of applications within the first day or two of posting. That volume is one reason screening tools and clear stage tracking become more important as hiring activity picks up, not optional extras to add later.


Related terms: Candidate Pipeline, Job Board Distribution, Applicant Tracking System (ATS)


### Candidate Pipeline


A candidate pipeline is the view inside an ATS that shows every applicant tied to a requisition, along with the stage each one has reached, such as applied, screened, interviewed, or offered. It gives a hiring manager a live picture of where things stand without having to interrupt a recruiter for a status update.


Stage names, and how customizable they are, vary by vendor. If your process includes a stage a vendor's default template doesn't account for, such as a working interview, a reference check hold, or a second-round panel, the demo is where you find out whether that stage can be added and renamed, not just reordered.


Asure Recruiting's pipeline stages are configurable rather than fixed, so a stage like that can be added and renamed instead of squeezed into an existing one that doesn't quite fit. Every applicant tied to a requisition sits on one shared dashboard, so a hiring manager and a recruiter are looking at the same picture instead of comparing notes over email.


Related terms: Requisition, Disposition, Screening


### Job Board Distribution


Job board distribution is an ATS feature that publishes one job posting to multiple job boards, such as Indeed, LinkedIn, and ZipRecruiter, from a single form, so nobody has to build a separate post manually on each site. It removes the repetitive work of re-entering the same listing everywhere a role needs visibility.


Most small-business ATS platforms include distribution to a set of job boards at no added cost, with premium placement on certain boards sold as a paid upgrade for harder-to-fill roles. Ask a vendor directly which boards are included free and which carry a per-post fee, since this detail rarely shows up clearly on a pricing page.


Asure Recruiting distributes a posting organically to its job board network at no added ad spend, with an optional paid boost to a larger set of sponsored job sites available when a role is proving hard to fill. That two-tier structure puts the free tier and the paid upgrade in the same place most vendor comparisons look for them.


Related terms: Requisition, Candidate Pipeline, Applicant Tracking System (ATS)


## System Types


### HRIS (Human Resource Information System)


An HRIS, or human resource information system, is software that stores and manages data about the people already on payroll, including headcount records, job history, benefits enrollment, and time-off balances. It's a system of record for employees, not for the applicants who haven't been hired yet, which is the main line separating an HRIS from an ATS.


AsureCentral functions as an HRIS for SMB employers, centralizing employee records alongside payroll processing, with Asure Recruiting available as a connected ATS for employers who want applicant data and employee data living in one system, not split across two separate logins. Some all-in-one platforms combine both under a single database; others keep them as separate products that happen to share a vendor name, a distinction worth checking rather than assuming going in.


Related terms: Applicant Tracking System (ATS), HCM (Human Capital Management) Platform, Native Integration


### HCM (Human Capital Management) Platform


An HCM, or human capital management platform, is a broader software category that combines HRIS, payroll, recruiting, performance management, and learning into one suite. An ATS and an HRIS are both pieces of a full HCM platform, not alternatives to it. As a result, the three terms get used almost interchangeably in vendor conversations even though they describe different scopes.


Full HCM suites built for large, multi-location enterprises are typically more system than a growth-stage employer needs to buy, configure, or maintain. Most small businesses are better served by the narrower slice of HCM capability that actually matches their headcount and hiring volume, not modules built for a much larger organization. AsureCentral is built around that narrower slice: payroll, HR, and recruiting through Asure Recruiting, without the performance-management and learning modules a full enterprise suite bundles in by default. When payroll needs to work alongside a separate HCM or talent system without replacing it,[Asure's HCM partner payroll integrations](https://www.asuresoftware.com/hcm-platforms/) page outlines which systems it connects with.


Related terms: HRIS, Applicant Tracking System (ATS), Payroll Software


### Payroll Software


Payroll software calculates employee pay, withholds taxes, processes direct deposits, and files payroll tax returns. It's a separate system from an ATS, though the two need to exchange new-hire information at the point of hire so the same data doesn't get typed into two systems by two different people.


Whether that exchange happens automatically or by hand is one of the more consequential evaluation questions an SMB employer can ask a vendor, because a manual handoff tends to break down exactly when hiring picks up and there's the least time to double-check it.


Related terms: HRIS, HCM (Human Capital Management) Platform, Native Integration, Bi-Directional Sync


### All-in-One HR Platform


An all-in-one HR platform is a single-vendor product that bundles an ATS, HRIS, payroll, and sometimes benefits administration under one login and one database. The appeal for a small business is fewer systems to manage and less duplicate data entry across tools that don't talk to each other. The trade-off is that any one module may offer less depth than a point solution built to do only that one job.


AsureCentral combines payroll and HR in a single system, with Asure Recruiting available as a connected ATS module, so hiring, onboarding, and payroll share the same system of record and stop passing data files between separate tools bought from different vendors at different times.


Related terms: HRIS, HCM (Human Capital Management) Platform, Native Integration, Payroll Software


## Screening and Ranking Mechanics


### Knockout Questions


Knockout questions are mandatory application questions, such as "Are you legally authorized to work in the United States?" or "Do you hold a valid commercial driver's license?", that automatically screen out an applicant who answers no. They reduce the number of clearly unqualified applications a hiring manager has to review by hand before getting to the candidates worth a closer look.


Employers with high-volume hourly roles tend to rely on a small, tightly defined set of knockout questions tied directly to legal or licensing requirements for the job. A question unrelated to a genuine job requirement carries legal risk regardless of how well-intentioned it seems. That risk is exactly the reason knockout criteria deserve the same scrutiny as any other part of the hiring process, not a default template accepted without review.


In Asure Recruiting, a knockout question tied to a licensing or classification requirement, such as holding a valid CDL, links to the job classification carried on that requisition. When a candidate who cleared that question is hired, the same classification value flows into AsureCentral without being reassigned later by whoever processes payroll, so the distinction the question was built to confirm doesn't get lost between hiring and onboarding.


Related terms: Screening, Adverse Impact, Disposition


### Resume Parsing


Resume parsing is an ATS capability that reads an uploaded resume and extracts structured data, such as name, contact information, work history, education, and skills, into searchable candidate profile fields, removing the need to type it in by hand.


Parsing accuracy varies by vendor and by resume format, particularly for resumes with graphics, columns, or unusual formatting. Before choosing a platform, test parsing on a handful of real resumes pulled from your own applicant history. A vendor's demo sample is generally formatted to parse cleanly and won't tell you how the tool handles your actual candidate pool.


Related terms: Candidate Pipeline, Screening, Knockout Questions


### Screening


Screening, in an ATS, is the process of evaluating applicants against minimum qualifications before they reach a person for review. Automated screening relies on knockout questions and scoring rules; manual screening is a recruiter or hiring manager reading through parsed profiles directly and forming a judgment.


Employers hiring for high-volume hourly roles typically lean more heavily on automated screening, while those hiring for salaried or specialized positions tend to rely more on manual review earlier in the process, since qualification for those roles is harder to reduce to a yes-or-no question. Knowing which approach your hiring actually needs helps you avoid paying for screening automation you won't use, or settling for a platform that can't handle the volume you have.


Related terms: Knockout Questions, Resume Parsing, Adverse Impact, Candidate Pipeline


### Disposition


A disposition is the recorded outcome assigned to a candidate when their application closes: hired, rejected, withdrew, or offer declined. Dispositions matter beyond bookkeeping. They're required for EEO ([EEOC, EEO-1 Data Collection](https://www.eeoc.gov/employers/eeo-1-data-collection) ) and OFCCP ([DOL, OFCCP](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ofccp) ) compliance reporting, and they need to be captured in the ATS before a requisition is marked closed, not reconstructed afterward from memory.


Missing or inconsistent dispositions are a common finding when an employer's hiring records get reviewed as part of a compliance inquiry, which makes disposition tracking one of the more overlooked evaluation criteria for an ATS. A platform that makes dispositioning fast and mandatory at each stage is doing real compliance work, even if it doesn't get marketed that way.


Related terms: EEO-1 Reporting, Adverse Impact, OFCCP, Candidate Pipeline


## Compliance and Reporting


### EEO-1 Reporting


EEO-1 reporting is the annual federal requirement for employers with 100 or more employees to submit workforce demographic data, broken out by race, ethnicity, sex, and job category, to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission ([EEOC, EEO-1 Data Collection](https://www.eeoc.gov/employers/eeo-1-data-collection) ). An ATS with EEO data collection built in automates the voluntary self-identification step at the application stage without layering a separate process on top of hiring.


If your business is approaching the 100-employee threshold, it's worth evaluating an ATS's EEO reporting features before the requirement becomes mandatory, not after the first filing deadline arrives. Asure HR Compliance's certified HR professionals can review the self-identification data an ATS collects at the application stage against what an EEO-1 filing actually requires, so an employer approaching that threshold gets recordkeeping and reporting practices in order ahead of time instead of scrambling to reconstruct a year of hiring data retroactively.


Related terms: Adverse Impact, OFCCP, Disposition, Compliance Audit Trail


### Adverse Impact


Adverse impact occurs when a hiring practice, such as a screening question or an assessment, excludes applicants from a protected class (race, sex, age, or disability, among others) at a disproportionate rate, even without any intent to discriminate. The EEOC's four-fifths rule is the standard test used to flag it: if a group's selection rate falls below 80 percent of the highest-selected group's rate, adverse impact is indicated ([EEOC, Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures](https://www.eeoc.gov/laws/guidance/uniform-guidelines-employee-selection-procedures) ).


This is a legal standard, not an ATS feature, but it's directly relevant to how you configure knockout questions and scoring rules inside whatever platform you choose. A screening question that looks entirely neutral on its face can still produce an adverse impact result once enough candidates run through it, and that risk alone justifies periodic review of screening criteria even after a system is live.


Related terms: EEO-1 Reporting, OFCCP, Knockout Questions, Disposition


### OFCCP (Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs)


The OFCCP, or Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs, is the U.S. Department of Labor agency that enforces equal employment opportunity obligations for federal contractors and subcontractors ([DOL, OFCCP](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ofccp) ). Covered contractors have to maintain detailed applicant flow logs and disposition records, which happens to be exactly the data an ATS captures automatically as part of normal use, whether or not the employer ever thinks of it as compliance infrastructure.


If your business holds or is bidding on federal contracts, don't assume any ATS on the market satisfies OFCCP obligations by default; check first. Not every platform captures applicant flow data in the format an OFCCP review expects, and an actual audit is a bad time to find that out.


Related terms: EEO-1 Reporting, Adverse Impact, Disposition, Compliance Audit Trail


### Compliance Audit Trail


A compliance audit trail is the log an ATS generates automatically of every action taken on a candidate record: who viewed it, what stage it moved to, when it was dispositioned, and what reason was recorded. It's typically the primary evidence an employer produces during an EEOC charge or an OFCCP review, and it's much harder to reconstruct after the fact than to have generated automatically in the first place.


AsureCentral maintains this audit trail as part of Asure Recruiting's standard recordkeeping, capturing view history, stage changes, and disposition reasons automatically so a hiring manager doesn't have to document them separately by hand. That structured record is what supports audit readiness for SMB employers subject to federal employment compliance requirements. Federal recordkeeping obligations for applicant records exist under both EEOC ([EEOC, Recordkeeping Requirements](https://www.eeoc.gov/employers/recordkeeping-requirements) ) and OFCCP rules ([DOL, OFCCP](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ofccp) ), with OFCCP generally requiring longer retention periods for covered contractors, so find out exactly how long a vendor's system stores closed requisition data before signing a contract, not after you need to pull a record from three years back.


Related terms: Disposition, EEO-1 Reporting, OFCCP, Applicant Tracking System (ATS)


## Evaluation and Selection Criteria


### Vendor Scorecard


A vendor scorecard is a weighted evaluation matrix that scores ATS platforms against a defined set of criteria, such as feature fit, total cost, integration depth, implementation support, and compliance capability, so an SMB employer can compare vendors on the same terms, without relying on impression alone after a series of demos.


Weighting cost and integration depth heavily makes sense for employers who already run payroll on a named platform, since a poor integration fit shows up as ongoing manual work long after the purchase decision is made and the sales team has moved on. An employer already running AsureCentral, for example, would score Asure Recruiting on that same integration-depth line the way they'd score any other platform, since the connection is native and doesn't require a file-based sync someone has to maintain. Asure's guide to[how to select an applicant tracking system for a growth-stage company](https://www.asuresoftware.com/how-to-select-an-applicant-tracking-system-for-a-growth-stage-company/) includes a scorecard framework built for exactly this kind of side-by-side comparison.


Related terms: Demo Script, Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), Native Integration


### Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)


Total cost of ownership, or TCO, for an ATS is the full annual cost of the platform: base subscription fee, plus any per-user or per-requisition fees, implementation cost, integration fees, and ongoing support costs. TCO, not the base subscription price alone, is the number that actually predicts what an ATS will cost a small business over a full year of real hiring.


Vendors typically lead a sales conversation with the base subscription price, since it's the smallest number in the equation and the easiest one to make look attractive. Integration fees are one of the line items a TCO estimate most often understates: a native integration, like the one Asure Recruiting has into AsureCentral, generally adds nothing to that line beyond the platform's base cost, while a file-based sync built by a third party can carry its own setup fee plus an ongoing maintenance cost most vendors don't volunteer until asked directly. Get a full TCO estimate in writing, covering your actual expected hiring volume and integration needs, before comparing platforms on price alone. For a fuller look at the cost-versus-benefit question, see[Are Applicant Tracking Systems Worth It for Small Businesses?](https://www.asuresoftware.com/are-applicant-tracking-systems-worth-it/)


Related terms: Vendor Scorecard, Native Integration, Implementation Timeline


### Demo Script


A demo script is a structured list of scenarios an SMB employer brings to an ATS vendor demonstration, so the vendor isn't just running its standard feature tour start to finish. A useful script typically covers a sample requisition, a screening workflow, a compliance report, and an integration handoff, all built around your own hiring process, not a generic use case.


A demo built around your actual scenarios tends to surface integration gaps and workflow friction that a vendor-led walkthrough is designed not to show. The offer stage is worth testing literally rather than taking a vendor's word for how it behaves: have the sales team send a real test offer and walk through the e-signature step, tracked all the way to acceptance, in Asure Recruiting or whichever platform you're comparing it against. Run the same script across every vendor under consideration so the comparison stays apples to apples regardless of which sales rep presented best; the[growth-stage ATS selection guide](https://www.asuresoftware.com/how-to-select-an-applicant-tracking-system-for-a-growth-stage-company/) walks through building one from scratch.


Related terms: Vendor Scorecard, Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), Implementation Timeline


## Implementation and Integration


### Implementation Timeline


An implementation timeline is the elapsed time from signing a contract to going live on a new ATS. For SMB platforms, that's typically measured in weeks rather than months, though the exact length depends on how many active requisitions need to move over, how much historical data has to migrate, and how complex the payroll and HRIS integrations being configured actually are.


The most common source of delay isn't the software itself. It's incomplete data migration from spreadsheets or a prior ATS that turns out to be messier than anyone remembered. Cleaning up candidate and requisition data before kickoff, not during it, is one of the more controllable ways an SMB employer can keep a timeline short.


For an employer already running AsureCentral, adding Asure Recruiting as the connected ATS removes one of those variables entirely. The payroll and HRIS integration already exists, so there's nothing to scope or configure during implementation, and the timeline mostly comes down to data migration and requisition setup.


Related terms: Native Integration, Bi-Directional Sync, Vendor Scorecard


### Native Integration


A native integration is a pre-built, vendor-maintained connection between an ATS and another system, such as payroll or an HRIS, that transfers data automatically without file exports, manual imports, or third-party middleware sitting between the two. Native integrations are generally more reliable and require less internal IT support than custom API connections built after the fact by a third party.


This distinction is worth pressing on specifically, because "we integrate with payroll" can describe very different things depending on the vendor answering the question. Asure's payroll platform offers a native integration with Asure Recruiting, so when a candidate is hired, compensation, start date, and job classification fields flow automatically into payroll and HR onboarding, rather than just basic demographic fields getting passed along while the details that actually affect a paycheck still get typed in by hand. Ask any vendor whether their payroll connection works the same way, or whether it's a file-based export that still requires someone to check and correct it every cycle.


Related terms: Bi-Directional Sync, HRIS, Payroll Software, Implementation Timeline


### Bi-Directional Sync


Bi-directional sync is an integration behavior in which a data change in either connected system, ATS or payroll and HRIS, is automatically reflected in the other, either in real time or on a set schedule. It's the more reliable of the two common integration models, because it removes the data-lag errors that show up with one-way file transfers over time.


A one-way integration, where the ATS pushes data to payroll but nothing flows back, still requires manual correction whenever something changes on the payroll side after hire, such as a pay rate adjustment made during onboarding that the ATS never learns about. AsureCentral is built so that employee record updates sync across its connected modules, including payroll, HR, time, and recruiting, without manual reconciliation by the HR team chasing down which system has the current version of a record.


Related terms: Native Integration, Payroll Software, HRIS, Implementation Timeline
